title: DarkHydrus
summary: DarkHydrus is a small espionage activity set that public reporting described in 2018 and 2019 against government and education organisations in the Middle East, with Palo Alto Networks and other vendors publishing the primary accounts. Its significance is not scale but tradecraft clarity: the documented delivery chain used a document that pulled a remote template hosting a malicious macro, which in turn staged a payload built with a scripting technology commonly present on Windows systems, followed by publicly available post-intrusion tooling. Later reporting described command and control that abused a legitimate public web service, so automated traffic blended with ordinary browsing and blended further because the service was already approved in most networks. The group's activity illustrates several durable defensive lessons. Remote template injection means the email attachment can be clean while the harm arrives from a second location after opening, so filtering must observe document behaviour and outbound requests. Script based payloads mean process telemetry for scripting engines carries more value than file signatures. Abuse of public services means reputation based controls are necessary but not sufficient, and behavioural baselining of which hosts talk to which services at what volume remains the reliable check. Evidence to look for includes unusual parent processes for scripting engines, document processes making web requests at open time, persistence through registry keys or startup items, and outbound traffic to cloud endpoints at times or volumes that do not match user activity.

beginner.definition: DarkHydrus is a name used for a small spying group that public reports described in 2018. It targeted government and education organisations in the Middle East. It used documents that fetched extra code from the internet when they were opened. Then it ran scripts, which are short programmes that automate tasks. It is a small group, but its methods are used by many others.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every part of this attack is ordinary. There is a document, a script and a normal web request. Nothing looks strange, and that is exactly why it works. Teams that only search for known harmful files will miss it. Watching what documents do, which scripts run, and where computers connect gives you a real chance to catch it early.
howItWorks: A document arrives by email and looks like a normal shared file for work.
When the reader opens it, the document requests a page from an outside server.
That page supplies a macro, which is a small programme attached to the document.
The macro then starts a script that downloads and runs the main tool.
The group uses a well known file sharing service to send and receive instructions.
Access is kept for later visits, and the same method is tried on other computers.
beginner.example: Imagine a visitor at the office with empty hands; his tools wait in a locker inside the building. The front desk sees a harmless traveller with no bags and waves him through. Only once he is inside does he collect the equipment he came for. If you search bags at the door and stop there, you never see the real plan. A document that loads extra code from the internet works the same way.
takeaways: A document can load its harmful part from the internet, so watch what it does after opening.
Logging script activity gives you strong clues that file scanning alone will miss.
Ordinary cloud services can carry harmful traffic, so check unusual use of them.

objectives: Explain a two stage document delivery chain and why the attachment can look clean.
Describe why macro and script execution logging is high value for detection.
Explain what command and control means and give an example of blending into normal traffic.
List at least three log sources useful for investigating this kind of activity.
Explain why a small group using simple tools can still cause serious harm.
